try to define discrete parameters.

This is the killer. You use a variable named 'nil' without
defining it.

My guess without seeing your model is that you used an int

Stan doesn't support int params.

I was just copying and pasting from the box here: http://code.google.com/p/stan/wiki/RStanGettingStarted#Example_1:_Eight_Schools

So the model is:
schools_code <- '
  data {
    int<lower=0> J; // number of schools 
    real y[J]; // estimated treatment effects
    real<lower=0> sigma[J]; // s.e. of effect estimates 
  }
  parameters {
    real mu; 
    real<lower=0> tau;
    real eta[J];
  }
  transformed parameters {
    real theta[J];
    for (j in 1:J)
      theta[j] <- mu + tau * eta[j];
  }
  model {
    eta ~ normal(0, 1);
    y ~ normal(theta, sigma);
  }

- Andrew

On Tuesday, October 2, 2012 7:49:20 AM UTC-4, atzap wrote:
Really??  I thought the expected value of a Poisson has to be discrete (http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poisson_distribution)...
The expected value (lambda) can be any positive number.

The STAN reference manual (v1.0.1) also says on pg 122 that the expectation "n" has to be an integer.  It threw up an error that suggested this when I tried switching my missing parameter to a "real".

But this is a problem with the current implementation of Stan. The poisson() function in Stan expects the "data" to be nonnegative integers, which is a problem when the "data" are missing and the missing value is a parameter.

There are lots of hits on Google about continuous generalizations of the Poisson distribution. This guy

http://cmscience.blogspot.com/2008/04/mt-6-poisson-and-gamma-distribution.html

has a simple one, which just replaces the factorial with a gamma function. The comments ask him to show that the continuous distribution integrates to something finite, which he doesn't do, but I'll presume that is always so, in which case you could take the log and do something like this in Stan

parameters {
  real<lower=0> phyto_miss[Nmiss_phy];
}
model {
  for(i in 1:Nmiss_phy) {
    lp__ <- lp__ + phyto_miss[i] * log(phyto_miss_lambda[i]) -
                   phyto_miss_lambda[i] - lgamma(phyto_miss[i] + 1.0);
  }
}

Or, as the link above points out, you could use a gamma distribution for the missing values.

Ben

Let me first try to clarify terminology:

poisson(y|lambda) = ...

y: non-negative integer outcome (aka the variate)
lambda: non-negative real value

For the Poisson, the value of parameter lambda just
happens to be the mean of the distribution (and
variance in this case). And also the expectation of
any random variable distributed as Poisson(lambda).

Following BUGS, we call any unknown variable a parameter.
And y is restricted to integers. But y is not an
expectation, so I wonder if we're talking
about the same thing.

Stan is fine sampling lambda as a parameter.

Stan cannot (yet) sample an unknown integer y. Not
in any of the blocks. We're going to add sampling
in the derivated quantities block, but that will only
work to draw random integers from a distribution
like Poisson(lambda). You won't be able to use them
as latent responsibility indicators in mixture models,
for instance, because there's no way to transfer information
from the derived quantities block back to the model.

- Bob
